title: POC scoping - private networking & data residency - MedicaSys
summary: POC scoping focused on private networking options (VPC peering vs PrivateLink), region/data residency constraints, egress considerations and bench-marking plan. Agreed success criteria include latency under 100ms p50 for inference, cost targets, and data never leaving customer VPC. Next steps: provide security docs, sample network diagrams, run baseline benchmark on 10k requests/day workload, schedule pilot environment provisioning next week.
topics: POC success criteria (latency, throughput, data controls)
next_steps: Redwood to send SOC2 + network architecture doc (Alex) by 2025-04-11
Customer to share expected QPS and token distribution (Daniel) by 2025-04-13
action_items: Alex Chen - Send security package and network diagram - 2025-04-11
Daniel Park - Provide workload sizing (QPS, avg seq len, peak windows) - 2025-04-13
Priya Nair - Prepare benchmark script and baseline config for 10k/day workload - 2025-04-15
Kevin Wu - Share egress policy and approval process for PrivateLink - 2025-04-14
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Alex from Redwood, joining me is Priya our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Daniel Park: Good, thanks. We have Sara, Kevin and Maya on the line as well.
[00:12] Sara López: Hi all.
[00:14] Priya Nair: Great, quick agenda — we want to run through private networking options, confirm data residency needs, and scope POC success criteria and benchmarks. Is that right on your side?
[00:23] Maya Patel: Yes that's the right set. We're particularly concerned about data ever leaving our VPC and also latency for API calls from our EU region.
[00:31] Kevin Wu: And egress — we have strict egress controls, any solution that requires routing traffic through a public IP will need legal review.
[00:38] Alex Chen: Totally understood. For private connectivity we typically offer two main patterns: VPC peering (or VPC/VNet peering) and provider-managed PrivateLink/Private Endpoint style (AWS PrivateLink, Azure Private Endpoint). There's also our Redwood Private deployment option where control plane is customer-managed in the VPC.
[00:51] Daniel Park: Can you walk through tradeoffs? Which is simpler to set up, which is more restrictive?
[00:57] Priya Nair: Sure. Peering is usually simplest for intra-cloud — it's a layer 3 route between VPCs. It can be quicker but it means routing and security groups must be configured carefully; you also need to consider cross-account peering. PrivateLink, on the other hand, front-ends traffic to an endpoint in your VPC so you don't need route changes; it's often easier for strict egress policies because traffic stays on the provider backbone.
[01:20] Sara López: PrivateLink sounds better for our security posture. But what about cross-region? Our data residency is EU-only, so we need endpoints in eu-west-1.
[01:29] Priya Nair: We can provision region-local endpoints. Redwood Hosted API also supports regionalized endpoints. For Private deployments we can deploy control plane and inference in your VPC in eu-west-1 — that's the most strict approach for residency.
[01:41] Kevin Wu: If we do PrivateLink, are there any egress charges to us? Our finance team will want to understand cost delta.
[01:47] Alex Chen: Good point. PrivateLink typically has per-GB data processing charges on the provider side; also peering has data transfer costs depending on cross-AZ or cross-region. We'll provide a cost estimate matrix. For POC we suggest measuring egress in the baseline benchmark so we can quantify.
[02:01] Daniel Park: Ok. On the POC: our main success criteria are 1) inference latency p50 < 100ms (EU region), 2) throughput of ~50 QPS sustained with spikey peaks, 3) zero customer data persisted in Redwood logs/storage, 4) security approvals. Does that align?
[02:18] Priya Nair: That's helpful and achievable in our Dedicated or Private modes. We usually recommend Dedicated capacity for predictable throughput. For zero persistence — we have a configuration for no retention and can integrate with your KMS for request-level encryption.
[02:32] Kevin Wu: How does that KMS integration work? We require CMK in our account ideally HSM-backed.
[02:37] Alex Chen: We support customer-managed keys (CMK) and HSM-backed keys via AWS KMS. For Redwood Private deployed in your VPC you can keep full key control. For Hosted we can integrate with a dedicated KMS key in your account via cross-account role. There may be some paperwork for key access patterns.
[02:53] Maya Patel: For benchmarks — what load generator do you prefer? We have an internal harness but open to Redwood using k6 or a JMeter script.
[02:59] Priya Nair: We can run k6 or a lightweight python load runner. For comparability we'd ask you to share sample prompts and average token lengths; we'll mirror your token distribution. For initial POC we recommend 10k requests/day with 50 QPS sustained windows to capture latency curves and KV cache warm-up effects.
[03:18] Daniel Park: Avg seq length is about 512 tokens, with some 1k token analytics jobs at night. Peak QPS is more like 120 for a few minutes.
[03:27] Priya Nair: Good to know — the longer sequences will impact throughput and memory usage. We'll size the instance accordingly; for 512 avg we typically recommend a 48GB GPU profile in Dedicated or multiple smaller models distributed.
[03:39] Sara López: Can we do a run with quantized model? We need to understand perf difference and any accuracy regressions.
[03:45] Alex Chen: Yes — Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles; for POC we can run two parallel configs: FP16 baseline and int8 quantized to measure latency and cost delta. We'll include quality checks against a small eval set.
[03:58] Kevin Wu: Talk me through network architecture for PrivateLink option — who's responsible for the endpoint service?
[04:04] Priya Nair: Redwood will provision a service in our account and produce a service name you accept. Inside your VPC you create endpoints which then appear as ENIs and private IPs. From there you control security groups and NACLs. Traffic never hits the public internet. For some customers we instead deploy a dedicated Redwood Private cluster inside their VPC to avoid cross-account PrivateLink entirely.
[04:25] Daniel Park: That second option sounds like it meets compliance best but is heavier operationally. How long to stand up?
[04:31] Alex Chen: For a pilot environment we can stand up a customer VPC-hosted control plane and inference nodes in ~3-5 business days given IAM and network peering info. PrivateLink/pilot is usually faster — 1-2 days for endpoints plus verification.
[04:45] Maya Patel: We have an internal approval timeline — security signoff takes about 2 weeks. Can we start network prep in parallel?
[04:51] Priya Nair: Yes, we recommend starting network changes and providing a network diagram. We'll give a sample VPC diagram and Security Group rules.
[04:59] Sara López: Also, we need to ensure audit logs flow to our SIEM. Can Redwood ship audit logs to our CloudWatch/Stackdriver or a syslog endpoint?
[05:07] Alex Chen: We can forward audit logs to your logging endpoint or integrate with your Kinesis/CloudWatch via cross-account role. For Private deployments logs remain in your account.
[05:14] Kevin Wu: One more — is SSO supported? We want SAML/Okta integration and RBAC for operators.
[05:19] Priya Nair: Yes SAML SSO is supported along with SCIM provisioning and fine-grained RBAC. We'll include a template SAML metadata file.
[05:28] Daniel Park: On benchmarks, can Redwood produce a CSV with per-request latency distribution and token-level costs? Finance will want per-token cost numbers.
[05:36] Alex Chen: Yes, Redwood Console has token-level breakdown and we can export the benchmark results as CSV with latency buckets and cost estimates per run.
[05:44] Maya Patel: For the POC data set — we need to ensure PHI is never sent to Redwood. We might have to use synthetic data.
[05:51] Kevin Wu: We will provide synthetic prompts. Any debug logs you'd need will be scrubbed.
[05:55] Priya Nair: That's standard. For debugging we can pull request-ids and aggregated traces without payload.
[06:02] Daniel Park: Great. Let's talk success criteria timeline. We'd like pilot results within two weeks of provisioning. Is that possible?
[06:09] Alex Chen: Yes. Typical timeline: day 0-2 network config and IAM, day 3-5 provisioning, day 6-10 benchmark runs and tuning, day 11-14 deliverables and security pack for signoff. So two weeks is doable.
[06:22] Sara López: Who will be the primary contact on Redwood side for the provisioning?
[06:26] Alex Chen: Priya will own provisioning and bench orchestration. I'll handle contracting and security docs.
[06:31] Maya Patel: Can you list the specific metrics we'll get? p50/p90/p99, token cost, throughput, error rates?
[06:36] Priya Nair: Yes, the benchmark CSV will include p50/p90/p99, mean, stdev, requests/sec, tokens/request, total tokens, and cost estimate. We'll also include failure/error logs counts and traces.
[06:48] Daniel Park: On the subject of egress — our compliance team flags any cross-border traffic. We need to ensure no traffic goes to US regions.
[06:55] Alex Chen: Understood. We'll ensure all endpoints and infra for the POC are in eu-west-1 and that any control-plane calls are either region-local or go through your VPC. For Hosted mode there may be control-plane interactions; for strict residency the Private deployment in your VPC is recommended.
[07:10] Kevin Wu: If we go the Private deployment route, who patches and maintains the runtime? Is Redwood responsible or do we take over?
[07:16] Priya Nair: For Redwood Private deployed in your VPC, Redwood operates the control plane under an agreed SLO but can give you access to manage nodes. We include patching and security updates as part of the enterprise agreement, unless you opt for self-managed.
[07:29] Sara López: Cost question — Rough ballpark for a pilot with 50 QPS sustained and 48GB GPU nodes?
[07:35] Alex Chen: I'll follow up with a tailored estimate but ballpark monthly cost for dedicated GPU capacity of this size is in the low 5-figures; POC is typically pro-rated and we can provide a pilot discount. We'll send a detailed cost matrix comparing peering vs PrivateLink vs Private deployment.
[07:50] Maya Patel: Perfect. Any blockers from our side to start network prep?
[07:54] Daniel Park: We'll need Redwood's AWS account IDs, service names for PrivateLink if we choose that path, and an initial network diagram.
[08:02] Alex Chen: We'll send those by tomorrow.
[08:05] Priya Nair: For benchmarks, we'll ask you to provide sample prompt corpus and token distribution and we will replicate the load. Also need a contact for network engineer who can approve security groups.
[08:16] Kevin Wu: That's me — Kevin. I'll coordinate network approvals.
[08:19] Alex Chen: Great. Any other questions before we wrap?
[08:22] Daniel Park: One small thing — can Redwood run a short latency spike test that simulates cold cache vs warm cache so we understand worst-case?
[08:30] Priya Nair: Yes, we'll include cold start, warm-cache and sustained-run tests.
[08:35] Maya Patel: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[08:37] Alex Chen: Thanks all — we'll send the security pack, sample VPC diagram, and kickoff calendar invite.
[08:44] Daniel Park: Thanks. Bye.
[08:46] Sara López: Bye.
[08:47] End of recording.

Notes on transcription: occasional word swap and speaker attribution is approximate. Some acronyms transcribed as words (PrivateLink -> PrivteLink, peering -> pearing) and minor punctuation inconsistencies.

Bench plan (included in transcript for reference):
- Baseline: 10k requests/day, 50 QPS sustained, 512 avg tokens, 120 token peaks. Run FP16 and int8 quantized variants. Capture p50/p90/p99, token costs, and egress bytes.
- Cold vs Warm: Run cold cache runs (start-from-cold) and warm runs to measure KV cache effectiveness.
- Residency verification: Ensure all endpoints in eu-west-1, verify via traceroute and provider logs.
- Deliverables: CSV of latency buckets, cost estimate, network diagram, security pack (SOC2, encryption, SSO configs).
